steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a blockchain security paper that presents a lightweight middleware bridging BRC-20 tokens on Bitcoin to Ethereum. Motivate the interoperability problem between the two chains, explain why existing cross-chain approaches fall short, and list our contributions and the main features of the design.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Bitcoin and Ethereum: value created, but isolated ecosystems
- Existing interoperability solutions and their limitations
- Contributions: a BRC-20-based middleware (MidasTouch) — design, prototype, evaluation
- Two design aspects: U shape, lightweight
- Note on the name MidasTouch

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Bitcoin and Ethereum: value created, but isolated ecosystems
  - Bitcoin: decentralized network for value transactions, revolutionized fintech
  - Ethereum: smart contracts and DApps
  - market cap as of July 2023 (CoinMarketCap): Bitcoin ~US$584.97 billion, Ethereum ~US$223.32 billion
  - both spawned many upper-layer tokens and DApps (market scales in the thousands)
  - UTXO model vs account model -> isolated ecosystems
  - users can't freely move tokens between heterogeneous chains; rely on CEX/DEX intermediaries, high costs and limitations
  - lack of interoperability hinders adoption and evolution
- Existing solutions and limitations
  - cryptographic techniques: zero-knowledge proofs (cite), hash-lock (cite x2)
  - external hardware: TEE (cite x2)
  - reconstructing the entire system: Polkadot (cite), Cosmos (cite)
  - limits: crypto computationally intensive, overhead; TEEs complex, hard to implement; reconstruction needs extensive changes, extra assumptions/complexities
  - -> impracticability, impedes wide adoption
- Contributions
  - lightweight middleware protocol bridging Bitcoin and Ethereum
  - built on BRC-20 (cite x2): experimental token standard on Bitcoin, akin to ERC-20
  - idea: interpret BRC-20 operations inscribed on Bitcoin (Bitcoin inscription, cite), reflect them on Ethereum; extends Bitcoin within EVM, Bitcoin assets in DeFi (cite x2)
  - MidasTouch design (Sec. III): communication mostly Bitcoin -> Ethereum; users call Ethereum contracts via BRC-20 inscriptions
  - prototype (Sec. IV): functional methods on Bitcoin and Ethereum sides, featured events in middleware
  - partial evaluation (Sec. V) on Ethereum testnet: scalability/performance vs committee size, gas usage per contract function, validator processing frequency; results match intuition; security and limitations discussed
- Design aspects
  - U shape: inscriptions on Bitcoin -> state transition on Ethereum -> receipt back to Bitcoin for settlement
  - lightweight: no extra participants needed; validators = same group as or subset of Ethereum committee
- Name: King Midas (Greek mythology), everything he touched turned to gold -> valuable connectivity effect

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Bitcoin changed the field of financial technology because it introduced a decentralized network for value transactions. Ethereum took this concept further by bringing smart contracts and decentralized applications (DApps). As of July 2023, the market capitalization of Bitcoin is about US$584.97 billion, and Ethereum is at about US$223.32 billion (CoinMarketCap). These cryptocurrencies created a lot of value themselves, and they also led to the development of many upper-layer tokens and DApps, which can reach market scales in the thousands. But Bitcoin uses a UTXO model and Ethereum uses an account model, and these structural differences have resulted in isolated ecosystems. Users cannot freely transfer tokens between these heterogeneous blockchains, so they often rely on external intermediaries, like centralized exchanges (CEX) or decentralized exchanges (DEX), which have high costs and limitations. This lack of interoperability hinders the widespread adoption and evolution of these technologies and limits their full potential.

There are existing solutions that try to make different blockchains interoperable. They often rely on different cryptographic techniques (for example zero-knowledge proofs and hash-lock), on external hardware (for example TEE) or on reconstructing the entire system (for example Polkadot, Cosmos). However these approaches have explicit limitations. Cryptographic approaches are computationally intensive and can introduce a lot of overhead. External hardware solutions like TEEs can be complex and hard to implement. Reconstructing the system requires extensive changes, and this brings additional assumptions and complexities. So current solutions are impractical to various degrees, and this impedes their wide adoption.

Contributions. To fill these gaps, we propose a new lightweight middleware protocol to bridge Bitcoin and Ethereum. The middleware uses BRC-20, which is an experimental standard for digital tokens on the Bitcoin network, similar to Ethereum's ERC-20. Our idea is to interpret the BRC-20 operations that are inscribed on Bitcoin's blockchain (also called Bitcoin inscription) and reflect them on the Ethereum network. This extends Bitcoin's functionalities within Ethereum's EVM and makes it possible to integrate Bitcoin assets in DeFi applications. We reach this goal with the following steps:

- MidasTouch (Sec. III): lightweight middleware bridging Bitcoin and Ethereum; communication mostly Bitcoin -> Ethereum; users interact with Ethereum smart contracts through BRC-20 inscriptions
- prototype (Sec. IV): functional methods on Bitcoin and Ethereum sides + featured events in the middleware; insights into key operations
- partial evaluation (Sec. V), smart contract operations on Ethereum testnet: scalability/performance vs committee size, gas usage per contract function, validator processing frequency; matches intuitive expectations; security and limitations discussed
- two more design aspects:
  - U shape: inscriptions on Bitcoin -> state transition in Ethereum -> receipt back to Bitcoin for settlement
  - lightweight: no extra participants; validators = same group as or subset of Ethereum committee
- ♠ name: King Midas, everything he touched turned to gold -> valuable connectivity effect

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Bitcoin changed the field of financial technology because it introduced a decentralized network for value transactions. Ethereum took this concept further by bringing smart contracts and decentralized applications (DApps). As of July 2023, the market capitalization of Bitcoin is about US$584.97 billion, and Ethereum is at about US$223.32 billion (CoinMarketCap). These cryptocurrencies created a lot of value themselves, and they also led to the development of many upper-layer tokens and DApps, which can reach market scales in the thousands. But Bitcoin uses a UTXO model and Ethereum uses an account model, and these structural differences have resulted in isolated ecosystems. Users cannot freely transfer tokens between these heterogeneous blockchains, so they often rely on external intermediaries, like centralized exchanges (CEX) or decentralized exchanges (DEX), which have high costs and limitations. This lack of interoperability hinders the widespread adoption and evolution of these technologies and limits their full potential.

There are existing solutions that try to make different blockchains interoperable. They often rely on different cryptographic techniques (for example zero-knowledge proofs and hash-lock), on external hardware (for example TEE) or on reconstructing the entire system (for example Polkadot, Cosmos). However these approaches have explicit limitations. Cryptographic approaches are computationally intensive and can introduce a lot of overhead. External hardware solutions like TEEs can be complex and hard to implement. Reconstructing the system requires extensive changes, and this brings additional assumptions and complexities. So current solutions are impractical to various degrees, and this impedes their wide adoption.

Contributions. To fill these gaps, we propose a new lightweight middleware protocol to bridge Bitcoin and Ethereum. The middleware uses BRC-20, which is an experimental standard for digital tokens on the Bitcoin network, similar to Ethereum's ERC-20. Our idea is to interpret the BRC-20 operations that are inscribed on Bitcoin's blockchain (also called Bitcoin inscription) and reflect them on the Ethereum network. This extends Bitcoin's functionalities within Ethereum's EVM and makes it possible to integrate Bitcoin assets in DeFi applications. We reach this goal with the following steps:

- We present a lightweight middleware, MidasTouch (Sec. III), to bridge the Bitcoin network and the Ethereum network. MidasTouch allows seamless communication between these networks (mostly from Bitcoin to Ethereum), and it lets users interact with Ethereum smart contracts through Bitcoin inscriptions as defined in the recent BRC-20 standard.

- We developed a preliminary version of MidasTouch (Sec. IV) to show how it works. The prototype implements functional methods on both the Bitcoin side and the Ethereum side, and also the featured events in the intermediate middleware, and it gives detailed insights into the key operations.

- We do a partial evaluation of how effective and efficient MidasTouch is (Sec. V), and we focus on the smart contract-related operations on the Ethereum testnet. The evaluation looks at three aspects: scalability and performance with different committee sizes, gas usage for different contract functionalities, and how often validators process requests. The results give insights into how the system behaves in different scenarios, and they match people's intuitive expectations. We also discuss the security aspects and the potential limitations.

There are two more aspects of our design that we want to emphasize:

- U shape. The workflow in our design has the shape of a "U". Users start their requests by putting inscriptions on the Bitcoin network. The action on the inscriptions triggers a state transition in Ethereum. At the end, the Ethereum contract gives a receipt back to Bitcoin, and this receipt is a record for the settlement process.

- Lightweight. Running the middleware, which is maintained by validators, does not inherently need any extra participants. The validators that maintain our middleware can be the same group as the Ethereum committee or a subset of it.

♠ We call the task done by our middleware MidasTouch (see our title) as a metaphor. It comes from the tale in Greek mythology where everything King Midas touched turned to gold, which symbolizes a valuable connectivity effect.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The emergence of Bitcoin revolutionized the field of financial technology by introducing a decentralized network for value transactions. Ethereum advanced this concept further by bringing smart contracts and decentralized applications (DApps). As of July 2023, the market capitalization of Bitcoin is approximately US$584.97 billion, while Ethereum stands at around US$223.32 billion (CoinMarketCap). These cryptocurrencies have not only created significant value themselves but have also paved the way for numerous upper-layer tokens and DApps, which can reach market scales in the thousands. However, the structural differences between Bitcoin's UTXO model and Ethereum's account model have resulted in isolated ecosystems. Users cannot freely transfer tokens between these heterogeneous blockchains and often rely on external intermediaries, such as centralized exchanges (CEX) or decentralized exchanges (DEX), which come with high costs and limitations. This lack of interoperability hinders the widespread adoption and evolution of these technologies and limits their full potential.

Existing solutions have tried to facilitate interoperability among different blockchains. They often rely on various cryptographic techniques (e.g., zero-knowledge proofs [1] and hash-lock [2] [3]), external hardware (e.g., TEE [4] [5]) or reconstructing the entire system (e.g., Polkadot [6], Cosmos [7]). However, these approaches have explicit limitations. Cryptographic approaches are computationally intensive and may introduce significant overhead. External hardware solutions like TEEs can be complex and difficult to implement. Reconstructing the system requires extensive changes, which bring additional assumptions and complexities. As a result, current solutions suffer from various degrees of impracticability, which impedes their wide adoption.

Contributions. To fill the gaps, we propose a lightweight middleware protocol designed to bridge the gap between Bitcoin and Ethereum. The middleware takes advantage of BRC-20 [8] [9], an experimental standard for digital tokens on the Bitcoin network akin to Ethereum's ERC-20. Our idea is to interpret the BRC-20 operations inscribed on Bitcoin's blockchain (a.k.a., Bitcoin inscription [10]) and reflect them on the Ethereum network, extending Bitcoin's functionalities within Ethereum's EVM and making it possible to integrate Bitcoin assets in DeFi applications [11] [12]. We approach the goal through the following steps:

- We present a lightweight middleware, MidasTouch (Sec. III), designed to bridge the Bitcoin network and the Ethereum network. MidasTouch enables seamless communication (mainly from Bitcoin to Ethereum) between these networks, allowing users to interact with Ethereum smart contracts through Bitcoin inscriptions defined in the recent BRC-20 standard.

- We have developed a preliminary version of MidasTouch (Sec. IV) to demonstrate its functionality. The prototype implements functional methods on both the Bitcoin and Ethereum sides as well as the featured events in the intermediate middleware, providing detailed insights into key operations.

- We conduct a partial evaluation of the effectiveness and efficiency of MidasTouch (Sec. V), focusing on smart contract-related operations on the Ethereum testnet. Our evaluation covers three key aspects: scalability and performance with varying committee sizes, gas usage for different contract functionalities, and the frequency with which validators process requests. The results give insights into the system's behavior under different scenarios, which align with people's intuitive expectations. We also discuss the security aspects and potential limitations.

We emphasize two additional aspects of our design:

- U shape. The workflow of our design takes the shape of a "U": users initiate their requests by inputting inscriptions on the Bitcoin network. The action on inscriptions triggers a state transition within Ethereum. Finally, the Ethereum contract furnishes a receipt to Bitcoin, which serves as a record for the settlement process.

- Lightweight. Operating the validator-maintained middleware does not inherently require supplementary participants. The validators who maintain our middleware can either be the same group as the Ethereum committee or a subset of it.

♠ We metaphorically call the task achieved by our middleware MidasTouch (cf. our title), inspired by the tale in Greek mythology: everything King Midas touched turned to gold, symbolizing a valuable connectivity effect.

References:
[1] T. Xie, J. Zhang, Z. Cheng, F. Zhang, Y. Zhang, Y. Jia, D. Boneh, and D. Song, “zkbridge: Trustless cross-chain bridges made practical,” in Proceedings of the ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS) , 2022, pp. 3003–3017.
[2] S. Wadhwa, J. Stöter et al. , “He-HTLC: Revisiting incentives in HTLC,” Network and Distributed System Security (NDSS) , 2023.
[3] D. Balazs, “Herdius whitepaper,” https://herdius.com/whitepaper/Herdius_Technical_Paper.pdf , 2017.
[4] I. Bentov, Y. Ji, F. Zhang, L. Breidenbach, P. Daian, and A. Juels, “Tesseract: Real-time cryptocurrency exchange using trusted hardware,” in Proceedings of the ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS) , 2019, pp. 1521–1538.
[5] Y. Lan, J. Gao, Y. Li, K. Wang, Y. Zhu, and Z. Chen, “Trustcross: Enabling confidential interoperability across blockchains using trusted hardware,” in International Conference on Blockchain Technology and Applications (ICBTA) , 2021, pp. 17–23.
[6] G. Wood, “Polkadot: Vision for a heterogeneous multi-chain framework,” White paper , vol. 21, no. 2327, p. 4662, 2016.
[7] J. Kwon and E. Buchman, “Cosmos whitepaper,” A Netw. Distrib. Ledgers , vol. 27, 2019.
[8] Anonymous, “BRC-20 experiment,” https://domo-2.gitbook.io/brc-20-experiment/ , 2023.
[9] B. Research, “BRC-20 tokens: A primer,” https://research.binance.com/static/pdf/BRC-20%20Tokens%20-%20A%20Primer.pdf , 2023.
[10] N. Li, M. Qi et al. , “Bitcoin inscriptions: Foundations and beyond,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2401.17581 , 2024.
[11] S. Werner, D. Perez, L. Gudgeon, A. Klages-Mundt, D. Harz, and W. Knottenbelt, “SoK: Decentralized finance ( DeFi),” in Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Advances in Financial Technologies (AFT) , 2022, pp. 30–46.
